content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes model-agnostic meta-attack to learn to generate attack gradients with true gradient update sequences with an RNN. It introduces meta-learning based approach to help trained attacks generalize well to unseen defenses.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
### Strengths
* The method appears to be competitive against strong baselines such as AA and ODI while using fewer iterations.
* The attack can generalize well to unseen models with meta-learning.

### Weaknesses
* The method is overall too complicated for a relatively small improvement. I do not believe a few decimal point changes in the attack accuracy percentages merit the complexity to implement this. Past competitions on white-box attacks [1] show that all you need is a good surrogate loss function, a good initialization, and a good gradient descent strategy.
* The results are notably missing recent SOTA attacks [2-4], and [3,4] are learned approaches. Upon comparison, they may report stronger attacks for some defenses with fewer iterations while being simpler. 
* Presumably, the gradient proposal model as defined in eq. (3) takes a true gradient as its input. I wonder what would happen if the true gradient is all zero, would it nullify the attack, or simply suggest a sensible starting point? Some flawed defenses may produce zero-valued gradients as a result of floating-point underflow to circumvent traditional PGD attacks.


[1]: Dong et al., Adversarial Attacks on ML Defense Models Competition, https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08042.

[2]: Liu et al., Practical Evaluation of Adversarial Robustness via Adaptive Auto Attack, CVPR 2022.

[3]: Yu et al., LAFEAT: Piercing Through Adversarial Defenses with Latent Features, CVPR 2021.

[4]: Mao et al., Composite Adversarial Attacks, AAAI 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
### Novelty
The paper’s idea is somewhat similar to [5], which also adopts meta-learning for improved adversarial transferability. This paper appears to extend this idea to gradient proposal with an RNN taking true gradient inputs.

[5]: Yuan et al., Meta Gradient Adversarial Attack, ICCV 2021.

### Quality
The paper is generally well written with few grammatical issues.

### Reproducibility
* Can you provide a training curve on the objective $\mathcal{J}$?
content.summary_of_the_review: While the method is effective, it is not clear if learning is actually necessary to improve robustness evaluation.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a new attack algorithm named MAMA, in order to better evaluate adversarial robustness. The main comparison target is AutoAttack. Different from previous methods that involve many hand-designed components, this work attempts to make the algorithm automatically learned. This manuscript first introduces RNNs for learning the attack algorithm in a meta-learning manner. To make the learned attack algorithm agnostic to the victim model for generalization capability,  the MAMA training algorithm is designed. Experiments are conducted on the commonly used CIFAR-10 dataset. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

-The motivation is clear: replace manually designed optimizer with a learned model for better performance.
-The paper is well-organized. It's a solid incremental work with easy-to-follow organization.
-the proposed method outperforms the previous methods. Even if this paper has missed A^3 (NeurIPS 21, will mention again later), it still seems better.
-the idea behind the design of the proposed method is simple and straghtfroward.
-for the rest strengths see the "clarity, ..." section.

Weaknesses

-[references, missing sota, minor] there is a newer follow-up of AA: Automated Discovery of Adaptive Attacks on Adversarial Defenses, NeurIPS 2021, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2102.11860v3.pdf. But the authors don't have to worry about this. In Tab. 1, row B11 of the mentioned paper, the A^3 performance is 60.01 against AWP, while in Tab.4 of this manuscript, the MAMA method achieves 59.95. So it seems that the proposed method is still better. I did not check whether the settings are aligned, and did not check all the numbers. I'd suggest the authors include A^3 in the comparison as well.

-[references, suggestion] regarding the last sentence of the 2nd paragraph of section 1, there is a very relevant reference: AutoDA: Automated Decision-based Iterative Adversarial Attacks, USENIX SS, 2022. This reference aims to search for black-box attack algorithms in a hand-crafted manner.

-[experiment, minor] The improvement brought by recent works have been smaller and smaller -- from which we can see the difficulty of the problem increases. Based on that, comparing very close digits without an error bar makes me not very confident in believing a true improvement. I know that adversarial training is extremely slow. If time is not enough, the author may only evaluate the most typical setting.

-[presentation, minor] please enlarge the font in fig1 a little bit. The current size is not easy to read in printed form.

-[design issue, minor] the caption of fig1 reminds me of the combinatorial explosion issue when there are, say, 10 defense models. How do we choose a sensible division in this case? Will the method design suffer from the combinatorial explosion? Or, say, will a increased number of defense models require a larger RNN model capacity and longer training time?

-[design, trivial] regarding selecting LSTM as the RNN: GRU (gated recurrent unit) is faster to train than LSTM. The author may try this in the future. No need to respond to this point.

-[unclear detail, major] cifar size is `1*32*32`. This is acceptable as RNN input dimension. However, imagenet size is typically `3*224*224`. I think the imagenet setting will be demanding of GPU memory to fit RNNs with such a giant input sequence. How are experiments in table 5 done given different input dimensionality? This is a major issue of method extensibility to imagenet, once it's unclear how the experiment is done.

-[ablation, major] the MAMA algorithm requires a set of N defense models. How sensitive is the proposed method regarding N? And how sensitive is the proposed method regarding the defense model quality? These are important questions for future adopters. for instance, what if we choose five methods instead of four in section 4.3?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
-[clarity] adversarial robustness evaluation is an important topic. This paper has a clear motivation to extend the attack search space by learning, compared to previous methods that involve manually designed attack algorithms. Specifically, the manually designed optimizer is replaced by a recurrent model.

-[quality] abstract and section 1 are easy to follow. Their content well-covered the content of the paper.

-[quality] a comprehensive but not lengthy background review is provided in section 2. Important related works are (almost) sufficiently cited.

-[clarity] in section 2, the relation of the method and other potentially similar methods is justified. for instance, that RNN model (I hope ICLR template could provide a ruler to specify line number, but the author know which line I'm mentioning) for adversarial training differs from the RNN model in this paper.

-[quality] the organization of experiments is clear. the corresponding section is easy to follow.

-[novelty] Replaced the optimizer in traditional attacks with a learned model in meta-learning manner.

-[reproducibility] seems good. there are python code and usage instructions.
content.summary_of_the_review:
This is a solid incremental work with good paper presentation. However, two major concerns make it hard to recommend acceptance at the current stage: (1) extensibility to imagenet is unknown and unclear. The experiment section does not mention how this is done at all. (2) ablation and discussion on the choice of N and defense methods are absent. Future adopters will be confused about the way to choose them.
My preliminary recommendation is weak reject.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new adversarial attack steered at the reliable evaluation of model robustness. Motivated by prior overly optimistic robustness evaluation of defenses proposed against adversarial attacks, BMA and MAMA are proposed as mitigations. The idea is to train a recurrent neural network to automatically learn an attack, based on a dataset and a set of existing defenses. The method is extended to also generalize to unseen defenses and unseen datasets. Evaluation is performed mostly on CIFAR-10, with a proof of transferability to CIFAR-100 and ImageNet.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths:**
- Interesting idea that seems novel to apply meta-learning for adversarial attack improvement and adversarial robustness evaluation.
- The topic of thorough evaluation of adversarial robustness is an open one, relevant to the ICLR community.
- Good overview of state-of-the-art in adversarial examples.
- Extensive evaluation of individual components of proposed method.
- Sufficient experiments comparing the proposed BMA / MAMA with existing attacks, on a wide range of defenses.
- Code provided.

**Weaknesses:**
- Limited robustness improvement over existing attacks.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality:
- Some comparison baselines seem to only be included at times. It is not clear how the decision is made whether to show some results or not.
  * E.g., defenses considered for BMA evaluation are all variations of adversarial training. Moreover, vanilla adversarial training is missing.
  * E.g., Fig. 5 and 6 regarding run time only compare a small number of attacks. Why not include the other attacks?
- It is unclear to me why Tab. 4 makes the distinction between defenses using $\epsilon = 8/255$ and defenses using $\epsilon = 0.031$, as $8/255 = 0.031$.

Clarity:
- The paper is well structured and easy to understand.

Reproducibility:
- Results seem reproducible, parameters for experiments are provided, and a code base is made available.
content.summary_of_the_review: Novel attack for improving adversarial robustness evaluation, with extensive experimental results. The main caveat seems to be the limited robustness improvement w.r.t. existing baselines.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
